items.title: 14 days in Dragon Shelter: A play by play of my first season in the Stardew-style farm sim where dragons help bake pies
items.author: lauren@pcgamer.com (Lauren Morton)
items.summary:
Day 1: Anybody home?

(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio)I arrive at my grandpa's overgrown old cottage alone. Where's he run off to? Apparently I don't know.
items.text:
Day 1: Anybody home?

(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio)I arrive at my grandpa's overgrown old cottage alone. Where's he run off to? Apparently I don't know. There's only enough time on day one to read several tutorial popups telling me what to do next (oh dear, that ta-dah noise is going to get on my nerves fast), cut a few trees with my axe so I can use wood to fix my bed, and go to sleep.

Day 2: There's always free seeds

Today I get to walk into town and oh, jeez, everyone here is Eeyore-level sad, heads facing navels and all. Even the music is depressing. The mayor tells me the town's in shambles and everyone's gone away and maybe I could help the couple folks who are left.

Well then, it's time to roll up my farm simming sleeves. The merchant wants berries which I can pick a ton of growing wild on my farm. The carpenter wants me to fix a cart by chopping wood. The gardener wants me to try growing wheat on my farm. Done, done, and done!

In the midst of doing all that though, I'm surprised by which things Dragon Shelter considers worthy of popup explainers versus what goes completely unexplained without even an indicator in the interface. Basic things like navigating my backpack are very fiddly and there's a "tips" button to find out which season seeds grow in before I buy them—important information that's available as a tooltip if you use keyboard and mouse but requires the unmentioned button press if you use a game pad, which Dragon Shelter recommends.

The tool animations and movement aren't clunky though, so that's one for the pros and one for the cons column on my normal gripes with 3D farm sims.

By about 8 pm I've acquired a shovel, watering can, pickaxe, wheat seeds, and a blueprint for an outdoor kitchen. I don't have the time or enough energy meter left to clear a spot on my property for it, so off to bed I go.

Day 3: Time for a jam session

(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio)I spend all morning clear cutting a large section of my yard to plop my outdoor kitchen onto. It comes pre-equipped with an oven, cauldron, matches, and a couple other basics so I can make some berry jam for the mayor.

The menu for queuing up recipes to cook is, like all the others, awkward and shabby-looking. I'm a bit of a snob about interface designs, sorry. It's just a shame the environments in Dragon Shelter are so cute and the menus don't match at all. In fact, what happened to the nicer-looking HUD that's in some of its Steam store page screenshots?

The tools bar in Dragon Shelter's earlier store page screenshots.Wild Forest StudioThe HUD in Dragon Shelter at launch.Wild Forest StudioThe cooking system is easy enough to understand, though. A list of visual steps for the recipe I've queued appears in the top left when I step into my kitchen:

Take berries from the basket

Put them in the fruit press and hit a button several times to mash

Pick up the cauldron and carry it over to add berries, water, and sugar

Place it on the fire

Grab logs for fuel

Etc, and so forth

It doesn't have the "oh god the food is burning!" hustle of something like Overcooked or the minigame-ification of each step like Palia, but I can see the promise.

Day 4: Cursed kitchen reno

(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio)What the heck? How do I add new cooking stations to my kitchen? Why is this not something that had a little ta-dah popup to explain it to me? I've been standing here half the in-game day confused.

Oh, I can't add stations while a recipe is queued up. There's nothing indicating that as the problem, but it's tucked into the "cooking" portion of the help menu. I would cook a berry pie for my current quest but my wheat isn't finished growing. Fine, I'll go to bed early!

Day 5: Dragon!

Finally I meet a dragon today! The liquid-y critter crawls out of the pond next to my house when it smells the berry pie I'm cooking. I feed it raw berries and we're best friends immediately. It doesn't seem like I can give it a name though. It's just "water dragon," bummer.

Cooking with my dragon friend is quite cute. It will try to do the next step in whichever recipe is queued up, like adding water (from its mouth, aww) to a cauldron for berry jam while I go grab another set of berries to mash for the next jar of jam in the queue. There are moments it gets a little confused if I'm working too fast for my dragon to pick up a step. It seems to work best if I start the process but then let my dragon finish a recipe while I jump ahead to begin the next dish so we don't step on each others' toes.

Day 6 - 9: How to train my pet dragon

I spend my first few days with my dragon pal growing wheat and potatoes, chopping wood on my farm, and cooking bread together. My dragon will automatically help with what obviously needs doing like watering crops right when we wake up. I can also queue up chores for it like chopping trees or rocks if I equip it with tools.

The carpenter offers to make me a trampoline for my dragon to enjoy and, boy howdy, if you thought cows playing with beach balls was cute in Fields of Mistria you're going to love a dragon bouncing on a trampoline.

On day nine the mayor tells me to start earning the trust of all the townsfolk with gifts and quests and I can use the "request board" to deliver them recipes they want like baked potatoes or bread.

Day 10: Standard farm simming routines

Alright, the "just one more chore" feeling of a farm sim has finally kicked in. Here's my day:

Water my crops

Collect sticks and hay to help the merchant fix his stall

Cook 4x baked potatoes with my dragon

Deliver one baked potato to the merchant so he'll fix his store

Deliver the other baked potato to the gardener to earn some friendship points

Feed two baked potatoes to my dragon because it's hungry

Sell produce so I can buy nails from the merchant to give to the blacksmith for a quest

I'm only just now noticing that there doesn't seem to be a map. Which is making it tricky to remember where to turn in quests. The bigger issue is how small the world feels. I've been just running back and forth between two areas: my farm property and the tiny town. Is there more to the world? I can't tell.

Day 11-13: The chores continue

In week two my chores continue: The mayor needs me to bring clay and hay to repair a dovecote so the village can have contact with the world outside again. The new rancher needs the watering dish fixed for his giant insect-looking critter. I've got to buy more nails from the merchant to fix the pier and I'm getting a bit suspicious of all the excuses the blacksmith has for why he can't just make nails himself.

I've welcomed a new alchemist, a weaver, a fisherman, and a bard to town. So many folks have come back but they're all still comically sad. The mayor proposes I cook food for a village festival, so maybe that will help the mood around here.

Day 14: It's very cute, but…

(Image credit: Wild Forest Studio)Dragon Shelter goes for the 14 day season instead of 28, so I've already made it to the end of spring. It seems that I'll be adding more stations to my kitchen to expand the recipes I can take on, but there don't appear to be a bunch of other crafting type stations that I'm going to plop on my property to create goods. I should unlock animal tending on my farm soon (aside from my dragon) so I'm eager to see that part too.

It's a cute game, but much smaller than I'd expected, so far. Shops don't have interiors (yet?) so I just talk with the owners outside. The villagers themselves really just deliver quests and don't have memorable personalities. If there's more to the world than just the two areas, I've no way to know yet. Its store page references "a vibrant fantasy world filled with magical biomes," but I can't tell when those other areas might appear.

From what I've seen so far, Dragon Shelter leans mostly on the novelty of doing chores alongside my dragons and the increasing demands of the cooking minigame as I add more stations. It doesn't seem likely to deliver a detailed story or intense profit min-maxxing of some other farm sims. It's just dragons and vibes, but they are good vibes.

Published Sep 25, 2026, 5:38 AM EDT

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section. He still quite hasn’t gotten out of his mid 00’s emo phase, and knows more about The Legend of Zelda and Doctor Who than is probably healthy.
Ewan oversees the content operation of ScreenRant's gaming output, working with a talented team of writers and editors to cover everything from the latest GTA 6 news to the indie games you need on your radar.
Former Editor of GAMINGbible, Ewan also has words at Kotaku, Den of Geek, NME, and UNILAD. He's appeared on various podcasts, including VGC's and BBC's Let's Talk About Tech.

We all know the famous Pokémon slogan. Gotta catch 'em all! But what began 30 years ago as a fun marketing term and challenge for young gamers around the world has rapidly turned into a terrifying prospect and borderline threat. As of 2026, there are 1,028 unique Pokémon species, including the three new Generation 10 starters. And with rumors suggesting Pokémon Winds & Waves is going to introduce 300 new monsters in 2027, it's about to get a lot more crowded.

Are there too many Pokémon these days? I grew up with the original 151, and I'm proud to admit I'm a curmudgeon who believes that yes, there are entirely too many 'mon now. Even so, that doesn't mean I haven't fallen in love with many of the recent Pokémon introduced into our lives. Let's take a look at the seven best Pokémon introduced in the last decade, shall we? We shall.

7
Alolan Raichu - Pokédex Number 26

I'd considered staying away from Alolan and regional forms altogether because it feels a bit like cheating, but I love Alolan Raichu, so I'm making it the one regional variant to grace this list. Also, it's my list so I can do what I want. What's so great about this alternate Pikachu evolution? It's an even cuter version of Raichu that surfs around on its own tail and has psychic powers. items.text:
There have been several mid-budget genre movies distributed by streaming-first companies that have underperformed at the box office recently. These titles — like Guy Ritchie’s In the Grey, David Ayer’s A Working Man, and the action sequel The Accountant 2 — have all been highly successful on Prime Video, even if they weren’t exactly theatrical blockbusters. There is, however, another category of mega-budget movies that have also gained solid traction at home, but can’t help but be categorized as box-office bombs. Last year, it was the action comedy film Red One, which grossed less than $100 million domestically against a reported budget of $250 million. This year, another sci-fi fantasy film has replaced it.

The movie in question, like Red One, was likely designed as a franchise-starter. And while there was some chatter about the studio wanting to proceed with a sequel despite the lackluster box-office performance of the first film, there has been no official word on the matter so far. The 2026 film cost a reported $170 million to produce, but it grossed only around $120 million at the worldwide box office. Of this total, roughly $65 million came from domestic theaters. Reviews weren’t glowing either, although some found its irreverence to be endearing. Now, the movie has passed a major milestone on streaming, which will only increase the likelihood of Amazon greenlighting a sequel.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
What Fantasy World Do You Belong To?
Middle-earth · Grand Line · The Continent · Camp Half-Blood

Pick your magic, your crew, where you want to wake up and who you would rather be fighting, and we will tell you which world you actually belong in. Four are open to you: an ancient kingdom living through its last good age, an endless sea full of pirates, a continent that pays people to kill monsters, and a summer camp where the Greek gods are extremely real and mostly a nuisance.

💍Middle-earth(Rings of Power)

👒Grand Line(One Piece)

🐺The Continent(The Witcher)

🔱Camp Half-Blood(Percy Jackson)

FIND YOUR WORLD →

01

What kind of power do you want?
Every one of these worlds runs on a completely different sort of magic.

ASomething ancient and half forgotten that came down through my family.
BSomething completely ridiculous that works in a fight and gets a laugh.
CNo magic at all, just training, potions and a very sharp sword.
DSomething I inherited from a parent I have barely met.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Who is travelling with you?
Nobody gets through any of these stories entirely on their own.

AA fellowship drawn from every corner of the world who barely trust each other.
BA crew I picked up one at a time, all of whom would die for me.
CTwo or three people I would never describe out loud as friends.
DTwo mates from school who are exactly as out of their depth as I am.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Where do you want to wake up tomorrow?
The best fantasy is usually just somewhere you would genuinely like to live.

AA high city of white stone with the sea somewhere far below.
BA ship under sail, with an island ahead that nobody has mapped.
CA rented room over a tavern, in a town I am leaving in the morning.
DA cabin at a summer camp with everybody else already awake outside.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How are you making a living out there?
Even in fantasy somebody has to pay for the horse.

AI am not, because somebody far older than me decided this was my duty.
BTreasure, and I am not always careful about whose it used to be.
CI take contracts, since people will pay well for what they will not touch.
DI am fifteen and this is all technically a school trip.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

There is something in the woods. What do you do about it?
All four of these worlds keep something unpleasant out there in the dark.

ASend word to somebody who has seen this before, then hold the line.
BWalk straight in, because it is interesting and possibly edible.
CAsk what it has been eating and what the village is willing to pay.
DWork out which myth it escaped from, then improvise very badly.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who is the villain of your story?
The enemy tells you far more about a world than the hero ever does.

AAn ancient evil that has been patient for several thousand years.
BA government that has spent a long time calling itself the good guys.
CA man who turns out to be far worse than anything I hunt for money.
DA god, or possibly my own family, and quite likely both at once.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What do you actually believe in out there?
Every world hands its heroes one rule and asks them to hold onto it.

ASome things are worth defending even when the odds are hopeless.
BNobody gets to tell me where I can go or what I am allowed to want.
CPick the lesser evil, and never pretend afterwards that it was not evil.
DMy friends come before anything a prophecy has to say about it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

A thousand years from now, how are you remembered?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your world.

AIn a song, in a language hardly anybody still speaks.
BAs the one who got there first and proved the whole thing was possible.
CBarely, and mostly wrongly, in ballads I would absolutely hate.
DOn a plaque at a camp, read by kids about to do the same thing.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

The Map Is Drawn
Your World Is…

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life
looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in
return.

The Rings of Power · Prime Video · Since 2022

Middle-earth

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and
somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right
thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

This is the only world on the list where doing good is understood as a very long defeat,
fought anyway, by people who will never see how it ends.

You are drawn to grandeur, to white cities and deep forges and the sense that almost
everything you touch is older than your entire family line.

The Rings of Power is set in the last good age before it all goes wrong, which gives
every quiet scene in it a slightly unbearable weight.

You would take the hard road, and you would take it on foot.

One Piece · Manga since 1997 · Netflix 2023

The Grand Line

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where
you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is
finding out what is over there.

One Piece has run for decades on one very simple engine, which is a group of people who
each want something impossible and have decided to go and get it together.

You collect people. Your ideal crew is a set of misfits who were each written off
somewhere else before you turned up and offered them a better idea.

The world is enormous and deliberately ridiculous, and the emotional gut punches land
harder because of that rather than in spite of it.

You would set sail knowing the map runs out, which is more or less the entire point of
it.

The Witcher · Netflix · Since 2019

The Continent

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The
Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the
people are where it all gets complicated.

Witchers get paid to do what nobody else will and resented for existing at all, which is
a trade most people would refuse and you would probably accept.

You have no real illusions about which side is the good one, largely because on the
Continent that question tends to have a disappointing answer.

The best of these stories are not about the fighting. They are about somebody with a
rigid code being repeatedly cornered into caring about people.

You would take the coin, finish the job properly, and be out of town before the story
got told wrong.

Percy Jackson · Disney+ · Since 2023

Camp Half-Blood

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and
you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as
everybody kept telling you.

Percy Jackson takes the oldest stories we have and drops them into car parks and diners,
which makes the gods considerably funnier and a great deal worse.

You would be the kid every school gave up on, who turns out to have been built for
something nobody thought to test for.

The series is genuinely about friendship rather than destiny, and it says so out loud
every time a prophecy tries to get in the way.

Camp Half-Blood is the real fantasy here: a place where the thing that made you
difficult everywhere else is the thing that makes you belong.

After 44 Years, This Forgotten Fantasy Classic Is Officially Coming to TV

Image via BBC

Over the years, the bloodthirsty lives of vampires have inspired
items.text:
After 44 Years, This Forgotten Fantasy Classic Is Officially Coming to TV

Image via BBC

Over the years, the bloodthirsty lives of vampires have inspired countless titles on TV and the big screen alike. From Buffy the Vampire Slayer and The Vampire Diaries to the Twilight franchise and the Oscar-winning Sinners, vampires have inspired stories in every genre, format, and, let's face it, quality. But while the catalog of undead stories is vast, the BBC's upcoming The Reluctant Vampire puts a comedic spin on a familiar creature — and now has a premiere date.

The Reluctant Vampire will premiere on BBC One on October 4 at 6:40 p.m. Based on legendary comedian Eric Morecambe's 1982 novel, the six-part series brings together an ensemble of British comedy stars for a coming-of-age story with a twist: its young hero comes from a vampire family, but he's human.

What Is 'The Reluctant Vampire' About?

The series, much like the original novel, will follow the young Val (BAFTA winner Lenny Rush) as he attempts to hide the biggest secret of his life: that he's not a vampire like his family, and is human instead. In the coming-of-age story, Val must learn how to cope with his newly discovered human side, all while dealing with the high expectations of his tradition-obsessed vampire dad, Victor (Tom Davis). Completing the family is Val's brother Vernon (Gabriel Nagy), who's suspicious that Val is hiding something, and their mom, Valeeta (Fleabag star Sian Clifford), who's the only one in the family who knows his true identity.

Published Sep 25, 2026, 6:39 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

For every great, and not so great, game that releases each year, there are a pile of projects that get canceled. Occasionally, some of these canceled games have great concepts that deserve to see the light of day. Sadly, we've just learned of a canceled Nintendo game that sounds like an absolute banger. Nintendo rarely makes a bad move but keeping a brand-new The Legend of Zelda adventure away from us gamers feels like a big loss. So, put down your sheikah slate, and stand with us in the graveyard of broken dreams as we look at what could have been.

According to a recent report from Insider Gaming, we were robbed of an intriguing collab between Nintendo and Ubisoft. In the past, this partnership has seen great success, with Ubisoft being responsible for the hilarious crossover game Mario + Rabbids Kingdom Battle, bringing many of our beloved Nintendo characters to life in new ways never seen before. Mario with a gun? Come get some! In fact, this crossover was so successful and well received by the fan base, that a sequel Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope was made in 2022 for the Nintendo Switch.

Riding off the back of that successful partnership, Ubisoft began working on a new Zelda game where the villainous Ganondorf was set to be the main protagonist. Alas, the partnership was dissolved long before the project reached fruition, and the untitled Zelda game is currently languishing in limbo. The project, which was codenamed Goliath, was first set to introduce a brand-new character before Nintendo suggested it be based around Ganondorf instead.

Ganondorf as the protagonist has such massive potential that it's a shame this project never saw the light of day. From The Legend of Zelda franchise, little is really known about what Ganondorf was like growing up. Bar his thirst for power and his hatred of pointy-earred guys in green, we really don't know what motivates Ganondorf. Learning what goes on in his head or perhaps how he became so evil could make for an amazing epic adventure. Then again, it's more likely that he was simply always evil and hungry for power.

The potential for what might have been feels limitless and users on Reddit are tripping over each other to theorise what would make a compelling The Legend of Zelda game featuring Ganondorf as the lead protagonist. One user hoped for the following:

I’m imagining it like the shadow of Mordor games, where you go through hyrule and build your army by infecting the creatures and eventually towns and hyrule castle

While another theorized:

The actual lore behind the triforce kinda works for a Ganondorf hero/redemption arc. The Triforce isn't supposed to be broken up into three pieces. It only does that when somebody with an "unbalanced heart" touches it. The pieces that they are lacking fly off and find more suitable bearers. If Link or Zelda touched it, the same thing would happen.

Option A: Ganondorf goes to seize the power of the Triforce, it breaks apart like it always does, and he sets out to retrieve it. In the process he learns about the "unbalanced heart" thing and goes about fixing that, becoming a better, more heroic person in the process.

Option B: Link or Zelda touches the Triforce, it breaks apart like it always does, and the Triforce of power flies off and finds a pre-villain arc Ganondorf. He sets out on a journey to reunite it and restore the sacred land. Since this version of Ganondorf gains the necessary courage and wisdom to unite the Triforce before trying to steal it he doesn't get twisted by the Dark World and having his prize snatched away by the gods' stupid rule.

Regardless of what a finished Ganondorf-led game would look like, it still feels like a loss to all gamers. Nintendo are generally great at quality control so perhaps what was on the table, just wasn't up to scratch. But with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake almost upon us, we don't need to grieve the loss for too long. Now, if Nintendo and FromSoftware can continue their partnership after The Duskbloods and bring us some Zelda/Elden Ring crossover... we'll all get over the lost The Legend of Zelda game from Ubisoft pretty quickly!

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

There's no doubt that the PlayStation 2's era of prominence was one of the most significant in video games as a whole, and there's a reason that it remains the best-selling console of all-time. Along that journey, we got some genuinely spectacular games, and it laid the foundations for a lot of the series that remain iconic for Sony today.

God of War, Ratchet & Clank, Kingdom Hearts, Devil May Cry, and Jak and Daxter all came along in the early years of the console's period of relevance, and most of those are still going strong (with others rumored to return). Now, one of the series that also served as an absolute backbone to the hardware offering as a whole is about to return, and it's going to look a whole load better than it did the first time around.

Koei Tecmo

In case you missed its initial announcement, Koei Tecmo confirmed the upcoming release of DYNASTY WARRIORS 3: Complete Edition Remastered, which is set to drop in less than a week at the time of writing, on October 1. As the name suggests, it's a return for the third game in the series, with fully updated visuals and plenty of new bells and whistles for the modern audience.

There is a growing crop of genre movies that perform exceptionally well on PVOD and streaming after they get a robust marketing push thanks to a theatrical run. These movies typically have a standard benchmark of around $15 million at the box office, which appears to be enough to recoup marketing costs and generate publicity for when they hit the home-video market. Some shining examples of the last few months are the World War II movies Pressure and Nuremberg, and the Jason Statham vehicles Mutiny and Shelter. Now, a new action movie is on track to join their ranks after overtaking one of the year’s most high-profile underperformers.

The new movie stars Alan Ritchson in the lead role, alongside Owen Wilson. It was released a couple of weeks ago by Angel Studios, a company that specializes in faith-based content, but has been expanding its scope with genre movies that happen to have religious undertones. Ritchson, of course, has cultivated a large following on streaming thanks to Prime Video’s blockbuster series Reacher, which recently concluded its fourth season. Ritchson’s new movie was given a theatrical release that coincided with the Reacher Season 4 finale, and the launch of the spin-off series Neagley.

Collider Exclusive · Action Hero Quiz
Which Action Hero Would Be
Your Perfect Partner?
Rambo · James Bond · Indiana Jones · John McClane · Ethan Hunt

Five legends. Five completely different ways of getting out alive — with style, with muscle, with charm, with luck, or with a plan so intricate it probably shouldn't work. Ten questions will reveal which action hero was built to have your back.

🎖️Rambo

🍸James Bond

🏺Indiana Jones

🔧John McClane

🎭Ethan Hunt

FIND YOUR PARTNER →

01

You're dropped into a dangerous situation with no warning. What do you need most from a partner?
The first few seconds tell you everything about who belongs beside you.

ASomeone who already has three contingency plans running and is calmly working through all of them.
BSomeone who reads the terrain instinctively and knows exactly how to use it against the enemy.
CSomeone who keeps their nerve and their sense of humour when everything is falling apart.
DSomeone who knows the history of wherever we are and what we're walking into.
ESomeone with the right contact, the right cover identity, and the right exit already arranged.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

You have to get somewhere dangerous, fast. How do you travel?
How you get there is half the mission.

AOn foot through terrain no one else would attempt — I move where vehicles can't follow.
BOn a motorcycle, a cargo plane, or anything else that gets me there before I think too hard about it.
CIn something that belongs to someone else — borrowed, stolen, or improvised under fire.
DFirst class, with a cover identity and a gadget that does something I won't explain until it's needed.
EBy whatever means are available — I've driven, flown, and once arrived by camel. The destination matters, not the method.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

You're pinned down and outnumbered. What does your ideal partner do?
This is when you find out what someone is really made of.

ADisappears into the environment, flanks them silently, and ends it before I've reloaded.
BCracks a one-liner, grabs a fire extinguisher or a chair, and improvises something that somehow works.
CProduces a gadget specifically designed for this exact scenario and uses it with infuriating precision.
DPulls out a whip, a pistol, and an archaeological insight that somehow gets us out alive.
ENeutralises the threat with maximum efficiency and minimum words — they were already three moves ahead.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

The mission is paused. You have one evening to decompress. What does your partner suggest?
Who someone is when the pressure drops is who they actually are.

AA bar with terrible lighting, cold beer, and absolutely no questions about feelings.
BThe finest restaurant in the city, a bottle of something expensive, and a conversation that is equal parts brilliant and exhausting.
CA local dig site, a museum after hours, or a long story about why that particular artefact matters to human civilisation.
DPizza. Bad TV. Falling asleep halfway through a movie neither of you were watching anyway.
EA debrief that turns into three hours of contingency planning that somehow becomes the most fun you've had all week.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How do you prefer your partner to communicate mid-mission?
Good communication is the difference between partners and a liability.

APrecise and minimal — tell me what I need to know and nothing else. Every word has a cost.
BDeadpan and dry — keeping it light keeps me sharp, even when everything is on fire.
CEnthusiastic and slightly chaotic — but always with useful information buried somewhere in the noise.
DCalm and controlled through an earpiece, with a plan that covers every variable I haven't thought of yet.
EBarely at all — silence is a language and they speak it fluently.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Your enemy is powerful, well-resourced, and has the upper hand. How should your partner approach them?
The approach to the enemy defines the partnership.

AInfiltrate their inner circle, learn everything, and dismantle them from inside out before they know we're there.
BStudy the historical pattern — every villain of this type has a weakness written somewhere in the past.
CGet them talking. The more they monologue, the more time I have to figure out how to beat them.
DGo through them. Directly. With as much force as the terrain allows.
EFind the one thing they haven't accounted for — there's always one thing — and make sure we're holding it.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Things go badly wrong and you're captured. What do you trust your partner to do?
Who someone is when you need them most is the only thing that matters.

ACome in alone, quietly, and get me out before anyone knows they were there.
BHave already been working on the extraction since the moment I disappeared — the plan is already running.
CCome in loud, come in fast, and worry about the collateral damage later — I'd do the same for them.
DUse every resource, every contact, and bend every rule until I'm out — they don't leave people behind.
ECharm their way in somehow, bluff through the hard part, and still manage to look good doing it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What does your ideal partner bring to the table that you couldn't replace?
A great partner fills the gap you didn't know you had.

ATechnology that shouldn't exist yet and the training to use it under any conditions.
BSurvival instinct so refined it borders on supernatural — and the scars to prove it's been tested.
CKnowledge of history, language, and culture that makes them invaluable in places where force is useless.
DThe ability to walk into any room in the world and immediately become the most trusted person in it.
EStubbornness that refuses to accept a situation is hopeless — and the improvisational skill to back it up.

NEXT QUESTION →

09

Every partnership has a cost. Which of these can you live with?
No one comes without baggage. The question is whether you can carry it together.

AA partner who never fully switches off — always watching exits, always calculating threats, even at dinner.
BA partner who gets the job done brilliantly but has the emotional availability of a locked filing cabinet.
CA partner who makes everything ten times more complicated than it needs to be — but who always comes through.
DA partner who gets personally attached to every relic, ruin, and artefact we encounter, which slows everything down.
EA partner who was not built for this and knows it — but shows up anyway, every time, without being asked.

NEXT QUESTION →

10

It's the final moment. Everything is on the line. What do you need from your partner right now?
The last question is the most honest one.

AOne line. Absolutely dry. Delivered like the world isn't ending. Then we move.
BNothing said at all — just a look that means we both already know what has to happen.
CA plan I don't fully understand that somehow accounts for everything, delivered in thirty seconds flat.
DA piece of historical context that reframes the entire situation and tells us exactly what to do next.
ESomeone who steps forward instead of back — because that's who they've always been.

REVEAL MY PARTNER →

Your Partner Has Been Assigned
Your Perfect Partner Is…

Your answers have pointed to one action hero above all others. This is the person built to have your back — for better or considerably, spectacularly worse.

Rambo

Your partner doesn't talk much, doesn't need to, and will have assessed every threat in your immediate environment before you've finished your first sentence. John Rambo is not a man of plans or politics — he is a force of nature shaped by survival, loyalty, and a capacity for endurance that goes beyond anything training can produce. He will not leave you behind. He has never left anyone behind who deserved to come home. What you get with Rambo is the most capable, most quietly ferocious partner imaginable — one who has been through things that would have broken anyone else, and who chose to keep going anyway. You'll never need to ask if he has your back. You'll just know.

James Bond

Your partner will arrive perfectly dressed, perfectly briefed, and with a cover story so convincing it'll take you a moment to remember what's actually true. James Bond is the most professionally dangerous person in any room he enters — and the most disarmingly charming, which is the point. He operates in a world of layers, where nothing is what it appears and every advantage is used without apology. You'll never be bored. You'll occasionally be furious. But when it matters — when the mission is genuinely on the line and the margin for error has collapsed to nothing — Bond is exactly the partner you want. He has survived things that have no business being survivable. He does it with style. That is not nothing.

Indiana Jones

Your partner will know the history, the language, the cultural context, and exactly why the thing everyone else is ignoring is actually the most important thing in the room. Indiana Jones is brilliant, reckless, and occasionally impossible — but he is also one of the most resourceful, most genuinely knowledgeable partners you could find yourself beside. He approaches every situation with a scholar's eye and a brawler's instinct, which is an unusual combination and a remarkably effective one. He hates snakes and gets personally attached to objects of historical significance, both of which will slow you down at least once. It doesn't matter. What Indy brings is irreplaceable — and the adventures you'll have together will be the kind people write books about. Assuming you survive them.

John McClane

Your partner was not supposed to be here. He does not have the right equipment, the right information, or anything approaching the right odds. He has a sarcastic remark and an absolute refusal to accept that the situation is as bad as it looks. John McClane is the greatest accidental hero in the history of action cinema — a man whose superpower is stubbornness, whose contingency plan is improvisation, and whose capacity to absorb punishment and keep moving would be alarming if it weren't so useful. He will complain the entire time. He will make it significantly more chaotic than it needed to be. And he will absolutely, unconditionally, without question come through when it counts. Yippee-ki-yay.

Ethan Hunt

Your partner has already run seventeen scenarios by the time you've finished reading the briefing, and the plan he's settled on involves at least two things that should be physically impossible. Ethan Hunt operates at the absolute edge of human capability — technically, physically, and intellectually — and he brings the same relentless precision to protecting his partners that he brings to dismantling organisations that shouldn't exist. He is not easy to know and he will never fully tell you everything. But he will carry the weight of the mission so completely, so absolutely, that your job is simply to trust him — and the remarkable thing is that trusting him always turns out to be the right call. The mission will be impossible. He will complete it anyway.

The movie holds a 77% critics’ score and an 89% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, where the crowd’s consensus reads, “With a winning duo at its heart, Runner may stumble over a few plot holes, but its steady stride and affable energy keep this action ride entertaining.” Runner has already grossed around $12.5 million at the domestic box office in less than two weeks. This is approximately twice as much as what Guy Ritchie’s In the Grey was able to gross in its theatrical run earlier this year. GTA 6 Gets Official Release Date Update From Rockstar Games

Published Sep 25, 2026, 5:03 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

The upcoming release of Grand Theft Auto VI really is going to be a monumental moment for the world of video games, whether you count yourself as particularly interested in it or not. Rockstar's hugely ambitious narrative release has been well over ten years coming at this point, and that alone has been enough to turn it into arguably the most hyped game of all time.

Taking players back to Vice City for the first time since the titular game, it's set to be a very different proposition from the original. The biggest differences are the timeline being moved forward to the present day (giving them a ton of fodder for their inimitable style of satire), and the dual protagonists, which falls much more into line with the experience we got in GTA V.

All of that said, the journey to launch has been far from smooth, but we are about to reach a very important milestone that should serve as a bit of a point of no return.

YouTube

In case you are one of the relatively few people who hasn't been following along with GTA VI's development journey closely, things have been a little bumpy. The game has officially been delayed twice (along with a rumored third delay behind the scenes), before the current big day of Thursday, November 19 was settled upon.

As first reported by GameRant, that means that September 30 is officially T-minus 50 days out from launch day, and while that is an arbitrary milestone in many senses, it is actually quite important in others. The biggest element is that it really marks the final point where a genuine delay is feasible. Obviously, they could push it back by a day, or a week, for last-minute unforeseen issues, but a big delay is basically impossible at that point.

That crossing point also comes at a time when Rockstar are really dialing up their marketing efforts around the game, and reveal a lot more about what we can expect as players. They simply wouldn't have broken cover in such a significant way if they weren't confident they could deliver the game on time, and that should serve as another mark that the 50 days out from launch marker will be just that.

At the same time, the developer recently revealed the $400 Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State - Vice City Collection, a collectible's set that features many of the designs from the upcoming game. Bizarrely, it doesn't include the actual game, which inevitably went down fairly poorly with the assembled masses.

In any case, it really feels like we don't have too long to wait to find out exactly what Rockstar have been cooking up with GTA VI, and it's safe to say that expectations are sky-high. Let's just hope they manage to deliver, or things might get quite toxic online very quickly indeed.

items.author: Natalia Keogan
items.summary: Taking even a cursory pulse-check of the pitfalls of modern technology—burgeoning AI sentience, data-center-induced draughts, massive quantities of unprocessed
items.text:
Taking even a cursory pulse-check of the pitfalls of modern technology—burgeoning AI sentience, data-center-induced draughts, massive quantities of unprocessed e-waste—will provoke an uneasy question: Did the Unabomber kind of have a point? This, of course, refers to the FBI code name (standing for University and Airline Bomber) for Ted Kaczynski. The man penned a 35,000-word manifesto entitled Industrial Society And Its Future, which, if it weren’t accompanied by a deadly mail bomb campaign, would likely endure as an articulate warning of the corporate-backed, man-made horrors of our current industrial hellscape.


Instead, Kaczynski’s legacy is inextricable from the three deaths and multiple injuries he caused as part of a calculated effort, between 1978 and 1995, to eliminate those he deemed responsible for what he saw as the fast-approaching erosion of natural and human rights in favor of technological evolution. The 1994 murder of advertising executive Thomas J. Mosser in North Caldwell, New Jersey (yes, where The Sopranos house is located) opens Janus Metz Pedersen’s Netflix biopic Unabomber, but the film is much more invested in the making of this murderer than the mechanics of his crimes.


Unabomber toggles back and forth between FBI agent Joanne Miller’s (Shailene Woodley) efforts to capture Kaczynski in 1996—ending what was at the time the longest and most expensive investigation ever spearheaded by the bureau—and Kaczynski’s formative time at Harvard as a precocious math prodigy (Jacob Tremblay) in the late ’50s. Between these two timelines, there is a palpable tension between prioritizing entertainment or accuracy. For one, Miller is a complete fabrication, a beguiling choice considering that the film delves into the very real role that Kaczynski’s brother played in his eventual arrest by the FBI. This version of the Unabomber—an unkempt, paranoid recluse residing in the Montana wilderness—is hardly ever seen. Instead, we get to know the man as a gangly, insecure student, completely adrift within academia and his general place in the world.


While not necessarily common knowledge, there has been quite a bit of research into the impact that studying at Harvard had on Kaczynski, particularly as it pertains to an ethically dubious psychological study conducted by professor Henry Murray (a flat Russell Crowe) that he participated in. It would appear that Unabomber largely leans on Harvard And The Making Of The Unabomber by Alston Chase (who attended the school at the same time as Kaczynski), which exposes the cruelty that the young man was subjected to while enrolled in the study. In the wake of the Korean War, Professor Murray sought to prove whether a man’s firmest beliefs can be upheld even under intense emotional stress. (“I bet you just look down at that tiny little dick of yours and just wish it would fall off,” sneers an unpleasant anonymous interviewer at Kaczynski during one such experiment.) As it turns out, efforts to assess an impervious American attitude ended up backfiring, big time. The key thesis of Chase’s book—the research of which includes intensive correspondence with an incarcerated Kaczynski—is that his 200 hours spent as a test subject effectively turned him against science and society writ large, pushing him to resort to violence as a means of direct action.


Yet the most compelling components of this text aren’t really present in Unabomber, which nods toward identifying details of the experiment but shirks from engaging with its psychological implications. Rather, banal story beats rely too heavily on Kaczynski’s dating difficulties and inherent introversion, and not how these already present insecurities may have been intensified. Indeed, even long after his capture, Kaczynski struggled with his mental health, eventually dying by suicide in 2023 at the age of 81. Instead of delving into the full breadth of Kaczynski’s psychological background, Unabomber is content with generic “abusive dad” flashbacks and simplified “frigid mother” anecdotes.


A Netflix dramatization of Kaczynski’s life, no matter the time period, would never be as faithful or scrutinizing as would be necessary to engage with the legacy of the Unabomber. Frankly, a project that actually engaged with his philosophy would probably result in a good deal of subscribers being put on government watchlists. But it’s nonetheless quasi-insulting that the film ends with a recorded interview with Kaczynski, in which he states, in a disarmingly soft voice: “My personal preference is to be depicted truthfully…To me, the main thing is to get rid of the industrial system by whatever means necessary.” For a film that is neither particularly truthful nor sympathetic to Kaczynski’s desperate need to question the cost of technological advancement, it’s an odd—if accidentally resonant—note to end on.

Writer: Sam Chalsen, Nelson Greaves

Starring: Russell Crowe, Jacob Tremblay, Annabelle Wallis, Shailene Woodley

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.
